title: AI safety & interpretability
intro: I’m a Ph.D. student in Computer Science at Columbia University, advised by David Blei. My work focuses on understanding what language models learn, measuring their behavior reliably, and investigating how they can become safer and better aligned with human intentions.

timeline.label: Undergraduate research · UNC Chapel Hill
timeline.title: Interpreting neural models for social good
timeline.description: Working with Mohit Bansal, I used interpretability techniques to investigate deep learning models applied to Alzheimer’s dementia and personal accounts of harassment and abuse. These projects used model explanations to uncover linguistic patterns and examine what neural classifiers had learned.

paper_summaries.alzheimers-language: Used activation clustering, pattern discovery, and first-derivative saliency to investigate linguistic characteristics of Alzheimer’s dementia and limitations of neural classifiers.
paper_summaries.safecity: Used LIME, saliency, activation clustering, and embedding visualization to interpret predictions about different forms of sexual harassment.
paper_summaries.metoo-abuse-stories: Interpreted neural classifiers of personal abuse stories using activation clustering to discover linguistic features.

timeline.label: Google AI Research Mentoring Program
timeline.title: Research mentorship in interpretability
timeline.description: Through the Google AI Research Mentoring Program, I was mentored by Been Kim on interpretability and democratizing deep learning models.

timeline.label: Applied ML Research Engineer · Meta
timeline.title: Generative AI Safety at Meta
timeline.description: I worked on AI-generated stickers in Meta’s Productionizing AI Research (PAIR) team, which led Meta’s early Generative AI efforts. As a lead engineer, I focused on making the product safer and more responsible, reducing stereotypes, and improving diversity in model outputs.
bullets: Used prompt expansion, fine-tuning, and large language models (LLMs) to improve representation in generated outputs.
In offline tests, increased gender diversity by approximately 30%, disability representation by approximately 12%, and skin tone diversity by approximately 6%.
Coordinated cross-functional teams on safety mitigation plans and roadmaps, led weekly syncs, tracked progress across multiple teams, and communicated results to leadership and partner teams.

timeline.label: Ph.D. research · Columbia University
timeline.title: Understanding and measuring language models
timeline.description: With David Blei, I study how concepts are represented in language models, how to measure them under distribution shift, and what model internals can tell us about reliability and alignment. My research connects mechanistic interpretability with probabilistic modeling and robust generalization.

paper_summaries.care: Introduces CARE, which separates shared concept directions from context-specific residuals. Evaluations include harmful-prompt refusal and toxicity, studying both measurement and intervention under distribution shift.
paper_summaries.robust-representations: Workshop work on CARE: extracting concept directions that remain useful for measurement and intervention across environments, including harmful-prompt detection.
paper_summaries.mechanistic-topic-models: Builds topic models over interpretable sparse-autoencoder features, connecting semantic analysis with controllable text generation through topic steering.
paper_summaries.hallucination-rate: Develops a method for estimating hallucination rates in generative AI for in-context learning, without requiring ground-truth labels for each generated response.

work.label: Exploratory project: text-based interventions
work.description: Tests the linear representation hypothesis by comparing how concept changes in text relate to changes in LLM activations.

description.text: AI for Health Equity Design Sprint

description: , building an AI research tool for a community partner, the Community Service Society of New York (CSSNY). The tool lets public health insurance advocates ask plain-language questions about New York Medicaid rules and get answers they can verify. The model is treated as untrusted: it has no internet access or tools, answers only from a curated corpus, and can select only labeled passages that Python resolves to verbatim quotations with citations. A harness adds query-only checks that refuse requests for private records or individual conclusions, a separate LLM review for support, exceptions, dates, and conflicts, and fail-closed validation. A document relationship map handles frequently amended guidance without assuming newer supersedes older, and a date filter supports historical questions. We released it as a research prototype for further evaluation, with a two-command local setup for ease of access.
